html:
The observatory that Ulugh Beg, Timurid prince and ruler of Samarkand, built on a hill outside the city in the 1420s. It was the greatest observatory of the Islamic world in its day and the last of the great medieval ones.

Its main instrument was a huge meridian arc, the Fakhri sextant, with a radius of about 40 metres, set in a trench cut into the hill and lined with marble, inside a round building three storeys high. With it the astronomers tracked the sun, moon and planets and measured the positions of the stars. They included Ulugh Beg himself, Jamshid al-Kashi and Ali Qushji. Their results went into the Zij-i Sultani. They measured the length of the year to within about a minute.

After Ulugh Beg was murdered in 1449, the observatory was wrecked, and Ali Qushji later carried its learning to Istanbul. The site was lost until 1908, when the archaeologist Vasily Vyatkin dug out the underground part of the arc. It is now a museum, and one of the best known monuments of the Timurid Empire.
sum: The observatory that Ulugh Beg, Timurid prince and ruler of Samarkand, built on a hill outside the city in the 1420s. It was the greatest observatory of the Islamic world in its day and the last of the great medieval ones.
